catalog_locator: p. 3 (§2.1 'Distinctive features of Côông', tone inventory, running from p. 2; §2.2 'Comparative comments', comparison table item a) and pp. 4-5 (last paragraph of p. 4 running onto p. 5) of the 14-page BLS download; verified and the 300-dpi scan (the PDF's own is font-garbled).
catalog_quote: [pp. 2-3, §2.1] The Côông of Vietnam has a high level tone (55), a mid-falling tone (31), and a mid-level tone (33) corresponding to the tones of the parent language *1,*2, and *3. There appear also to be some cases of a rising tone. ... [p. 3, §2.2 Comparative comments, table] Phunoi: a. minor syllables take the tone of the main syllable but has no independent tone — Côông: first syllable is often unstressed but has independent tone ... [pp. 4-5] Phunoi minor syllables possess a limited inventory of initials, schwa vowels, and a tone the same as the following main syllable. Côông word structure has some features of a weak first syllable; it is, for example, iambic with a somewhat shortened first vowel for many words. This vowel is frequently not schwa and the first syllable can have its own fully independent tone. On the other hand, the tone categories of the two languages also match closely in value and distribution.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (14 pp., BLS/eLanguage cover page + Edmondson, 'The Central and Southern Loloish Languages of Vietnam', BLS 28S (2002) pp. 1-13; text font-garbled, so verified against the held 300-dpi scanned the page scan and the rendered page scan, which I viewed directly). All three quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators: (1) printed p.3, section 2.2 'Comparative comments', comparison table item a: Phunoi 'minor syllables take the tone of the main syllable but has no independent tone' vs Côông 'first syllable is often unstressed but has independent tone' (items b, c: no voiceless nasals/laterals/palatals; no final oral stops, only /-m -n -ŋ/). (2) printed p.4 last para…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Côông is a three-tone language (55, 31, 33). In disyllabic words the rhythm is iambic: the first syllable is often unstressed, with a somewhat shortened vowel, and prominence falls on the second (main, final) syllable; unlike Phunoi minor syllables, the Côông weak first syllable usually keeps a full (non-schwa) vowel and its own lexical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged: iambic 'for many words'; first syllable 'often' unstressed; based on a field list of about 500 words; no statement for longer words or phrases.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (disyllabic word structure / weak first syllable vs. main syllable), from elicited citation forms in a c. 500-item wordlist recorded in Mường Tè, Lai Châu (1990s fieldwork). Brief comparative sketch, not an accentual analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Edmondson's data are Côông of Mường Tè District, Lai Châu, Vietnam (villages Bo Lếch, Nậm Khao, Nậm Pục, Tác Ngá, Nậm Kè) = coon1239 exactly. Bradley 1977 'Phunoi or Côông' actually describes Phunoi of Laos (phun1245) and treats Côông as a Phunoi dialect; Edmondson shows Côông differs substantially (no Phunoi-type toneless minor syllables, nasals for Phunoi voiced stops). Phạm Huy 1998 distinguishes two Côông sub-varieties (Xí Tù Mạ 'Silver' and Xám Khổng Xú Lứ 'Golden'); Edmondson does not say which his consultants spoke.
